    💡 Key Takeaways
    • These remain the earliest of early days but the blunt facts are there for all to see.
    • Not since 1974 has a Spurs team lost the first two games of a league campaign without finding the net.
    • This meeting with Newcastle United was, in the minds of those Spurs fans, meant to be a clash between a team remade by the transfer market and a team broken by it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    These remain the earliest of early days but the blunt facts are there for all to see. Tottenham Hotspur, the club that has spent around £380m this summer in search of instant improvements, have played twice and lost twice in the Premier League. After making eight new signings, they have so far scored zero goals and won zero points.

    Not since 1974 has a Spurs team lost the first two games of a league campaign without finding the net. The summer enthusiasm in this corner of north London is therefore already drifting away, to the sound of an alarmingly familiar soundtrack: boos from the home supporters at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

    This meeting with Newcastle United was, in the minds of those Spurs fans, meant to be a clash between a team remade by the transfer market and a team broken by it. Yet it was Newcastle, still adjusting to the loss of three key players this summer, who looked the more unified group and more organised team.

    Recent findings suggest that it proved to be a truly glorious evening for the visiting supporters, who not only delighted in their team’s victory but also in the struggles of Sandro Tonali. The £100m Italian, who swapped Newcastle for Spurs a few weeks ago, never came close to offering the sort of class one would expect for such a fee. That price tag is not his fault but it is his burden, and in time he will need to shoulder it more impressively than he did here.

    Roberto De Zerbi, the Spurs head coach, can rightly say that it will take time for his newly introduced group to develop the cohesion he needs. The worrying reality for Spurs, though, is that his opposite number had far less time to work with his players and far less money to reshape his squad. Matthias Jaissle appears to be a man with a defined blueprint, and an ability to convey it. Newcastle improved considerably after half-time, which spoke volumes of Jaissle’s work. “He is the best signing of Newcastle so far,” said Yoane Wissa of his new coach.

    "He is the best signing for Newcastle"Yoane Wissa praises Matthias Jaissle's impact at the club since becoming head coach 👔 pic.twitter.com/dX8nVknpKc.

    Recent findings suggest that for Spurs, so much of it would have felt painfully similar to last season, when they won only three home games in the Premier League. They played some pretty football in bursts, but not at the crucial points of the game. The second half, especially, was pockmarked with moments of despair. There was Mathys Tel’s free-kick that almost flew into Islington, for example, and Mateus Fernandes falling over when running onto a pass in the penalty area.

    Industry observers note that de Zerbi stated he was sorry for the fans and for the club, and suggested his team is not properly prepared for this campaign. “Maybe we are not ready yet,” he said. “For many, many reasons we are not ready yet.”.

    Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League meeting between Tottenham and Newcastle United in North London.

    Following consecutive 17th-place finishes in the last two seasons, Spurs are looking to enjoy a fresh start under Roberto De Zerbi without nervously looking over their shoulder at the perilous possibility of relegation.

    Industry observers note that nevertheless, Spurs’ season started disastrously last weekend as they fell to a miserable 3-0 defeat against Brentford at the Gtech Community Stadium. Since that result, Spurs have responded with an emphatic 5-1 thrashing of Charlton Athletic in the Carabao Cup, and also confirmed the signings of Savinho and Omar Marmoush from Manchester City. De Zerbi will be looking to continue this newfound momentum in the club’s first top-flight home match of the 2026-27 campaign.

    In a recent development, newcastle United have undergone a summer of significant change. Eddie Howe stepped down as head coach after nearly five years in charge, while Sandro Tonali, Bruno Guimaraes and Anthony Gordon all departed the club for lucrative transfer fees. Tonali welcomes his former employers to his new surroundings after joining Tottenham for £100m.

    Despite this upheaval, Newcastle demonstrated admirable heart in newly introduced boss Matthias Jaissle’s first game in charge, earning a hard-fought 2-2 draw with Liverpool at St. James’ Park on the opening weekend. Emotional tributes poured in for club legend Kevin Keegan as Alexander Isak made his return to the club he acrimoniously forced an exit from last summer.

    Recent findings suggest that newcastle looked to be heading for a victory after goals from Anthony Elanga and Joe Willock, until Lewis Hall, who had played excellently, apprehended Liverpool substitute Victor Munoz in added time to concede a penalty. Dominik Szoboszlai smashed a clinical spot-kick into the top corner to rescue a point for the visitors. Newcastle bounced back from these dropped points with a tense 3-2 triumph over West Brom in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday evening.

    A first Premier League win of the season is the aim for both clubs by the end of this evening.

    Kick-off is at 17:30, with team news on the way shortly.

    Ranking NBA's biggest winners and losers of the week: Knicks hit their stride, while Celtics take step back

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that let's call the last seven days the NBA's first parity week of the season.
    • In a recent development, the Western Conference is similarly crunched.
    • Sources indicate that you're expecting me to talk about Wemby's 50-point, 18-rebound, five-block, four-steal performance against the New Orleans Pelicans, aren't you?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that let's call the last seven days the NBA's first parity week of the season. Take a look at the standings right now. The No. 2 through the No. 6 seeds in the Eastern Conference standings all have exactly six losses, and while the Philadelphia 76ers hold a three-game lead for the No. 1 seed, they've done so behind a preposterous 12-0 clutch record. When they regress to the mean, we seem destined for an Eastern Conference packed like sardines.

    In a recent development, the Western Conference is similarly crunched. The San Antonio Spurs and Los Angeles Lakers sit atop the standings with identical 14-3 records... but seeds 3-9 are all separated by no more than two games. Even the Sacramento Kings got a win this week! The NBA has spent years tinkering in order to create parity, and right now, at least it's getting it. With that unofficial week of parity in the books, let's crown some winners and losers from the last seven days.

    Sources indicate that you're expecting me to talk about Wemby's 50-point, 18-rebound, five-block, four-steal performance against the New Orleans Pelicans, aren't you? That'd be the easy starting point. We could just as easily kick things off with Luka Dončić's shooting dip, as he has quietly shot roughly 41-31-82 in his past five games, bringing his ridiculous offensive numbers down to slightly more mortal levels and making Wembanyama, for now, the slight MVP betting favorite. Totally reasonable. They're both contributors to his excellent week.

    Neither stands up to what Wembanyama did against the Los Angeles Clippers on Thursday. He shunked. That's a word that didn't exist when we woke up on Thursday. It is now, hilariously, a signature moment of Wembanyama's young career. He has apparently dunked so often, so violently that he suffered a hand injury that compelled him to try, and succeed, to shoot a jump shot at the rim.

    Did Wemby just... shoot it from above the rim??? 🤯😲 pic.twitter.com/1YDxy8mwy8.

    According to recent reports, the MVP race is for the season. The ridiculous numbers are for the history books. The shunk wins the week. Any time you suffer and overcome a dunking-related injury by inventing a latest form of scoring, you win the week.

    According to recent reports, the champs have won five in a row and are 11-3 overall since their 0-3 start, but this isn't as simple as the Knicks suddenly looking like the Knicks again. Many of the early season problems are still persisting. Mikal Bridges hit the game-winner on Friday and still shot 3-of-12 on Sunday. Josh Hart missed all four of his 3-pointers on Sunday and is below 26% shooting from deep so far this season. The starters, as a group, are still getting outscored by almost 13 points per 100 possessions after struggling mightily in the past two regular seasons.

    Yet they just keep winning. There are obvious basketball reasons for that. Karl-Anthony Towns is getting every rebound, making every shot, and has readopted the playmaking hub role he thrived in throughout the postseason, particularly when it comes to assisting Jalen Brunson. The bench is thriving. Landry Shamet is shooting better than 45% on 3s and Deuce McBride isn't far behind. Tyler Kolek has a 61-to-9 assist-to-turnover ratio.

    In a recent development, but there's something deeper here, a resilience and versatility that developed over last season's championship run that is sustaining thus far this season. OG Anunoby has missed the past two games. Towns missed the Blazers game. Bridges and Hart play most of some games and only parts of others because of their early season struggles. Yet Mike Brown just keeps pulling the right levers, and the Knicks just keep figuring it out. Championships can bring about this certainty. The Knicks aren't quite themselves yet, but they have an internalized confidence that came from dominating the playoff crucible a year ago that's paying off handsomely right now.

    It has been revealed that it's hard to tell what we've seen from the Heat thus far this season that really deserves scrutiny. They started 0-4 in part because opponents weren't missing any 3s. They've gone 8-2 since, but they haven't beaten a single notable, fully healthy opponent during their active seven-game winning streak. No Evan Mobley against the Cleveland Cavaliers. No Jalen Duren against the Detroit Pistons. No Amen Thompson against the Houston Rockets. No... basically anyone against the Oklahoma City Thunder on Sunday, though in fairness, Giannis Antetokounmpo missed that game himself. Miami is something of a Rorschach test so far. You're going to see what you're predisposed to seeing.

    It has been revealed that but if we're going to panic during the shooting luck-induced losing streak, we're going to have to acknowledge the positives during the winning streak. The maligned Heat offense ranks in the top five over their past 10 games largely because Klay Thompson is shooting like Klay Thompson again and Giannis Antetokounmpo never stopped dunking like Giannis Antetokounmpo. Their core lineups featuring Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo are deterring rim attempts and giving up basically no corner 3s. Andrew Wiggins looks more like Andrew Wiggins since moving to the bench. As tempted as I was to give the third slot to the player development coaches for the Memphis Grizzlies after Cam Spencer's breakout 26-point game against Cleveland, the seven-game Miami winning streak gets the nod.

    Sources indicate that the Celtics were too clever by a half with their lineup decisions this weekend. They sat Jayson Tatum and Derrick White against the hapless Kings and then sat Paul George in the second half of that back-to-back against the Stephen Curry-less Golden State Warriors. They lost both very winnable games by a single point when they probably could have ensured a split and maybe even a sweep by aligning the rest. Throw in a 17-point blown lead to the Denver Nuggets and allowing a 40-point fourth quarter against the Orlando Magic and the previously 11-2 Celtics lost all four of their games this week. They're back with the Eastern Conference pack.

    Recent findings suggest that it's too early to draw any real conclusions, just as it was too early to crown them Eastern Conference favorites when they were throttling the Sixers two weeks ago, but this week was a reminder of some of the cracks here. Their best player is coming off of a torn Achilles, and their second- and third-best players are in their 30s and have to be managed carefully throughout the season. You can get away with never getting to the basket as a team when you're an elite 3-point shooting outfit. The Celtics haven't been this season, and we're now in Year 2 of Derrick White's 3-point drought (and, for that matter, arguably Year 3 of Jayson Tatum's). Mitchell Robinson will put together a few good stretches and then regress back into the mess he's been for most of the season. Boston has been nearly 22 points stronger per 100 possessions with him off the floor this season.

    According to recent reports, the Celtics, given their playing style and roster makeup, are vulnerable to the ebbs and flows of an 82-game season. When everyone's available and they're making their shots, they're going to look unbeatable. This week is what happens when they're not, and considering how frequently that's been the case for them in the playoffs, it's something the Celtics are going to have to learn to play through if they hope to make it through this crowded East.

    Slowly but surely, the NBA's cellar dwellers are starting to come around. The Utah Jazz won twice this week. The Chicago Bulls have won three times since Caleb Wilson went down, and they pushed the Denver Nuggets to overtime on Sunday. The Kings got win No. 2 on Saturday, but also pushed the Los Angeles Lakers to the brink on Friday. There is still a whole lot of misery at the bottom of the standings, but all of these teams can find small pockets of optimism.

    In a recent development, not the Bucks, who are now the NBA's last one-win team and owners of a 13-game losing streak. One of those losses came against Miami this week as their former franchise player, Antetokounmpo, throttled them for three quarters before they made the final score look respectable in the fourth quarter. They have the NBA's worst defense comfortably. Beyond a three-game stretch in which second-year guard Kasparas Jakučionis averaged 21 points per game, it's simply been a miserable season in Milwaukee, and it's one that could get worse any day now as the NBA investigates potential salary cap circumvention involving Gary Trent Jr. We all knew the Bucks would struggle with post-Giannis life, but this is worse than anyone could have imagined.

    Industry observers note that tyrese Haliburton has played four games this season at a roughly All-Star level. The Indiana Pacers are now 3-10 in all other contests, and ESPN reported Friday that Haliburton is set to miss at least another few weeks with a left hamstring strain. This is after a 19-win season played entirely without Haliburton a year ago. At this point, obvious as it sounds, it's simply become clear that the Pacers can't win consistently without their best player. That was obvious in a playoff context, but the regular-season implications here are starting to add up.

    Indiana is already six games out of a top-six Eastern Conference seed. Even when Haliburton gets back, he's probably not going to be perfectly healthy for the entire rest of the season just given his own history of durability concerns. The East's bottom four teams are thankfully so dreadful that there's probably a floor of No. 11 here, but Indiana will eventually have to pass someone -- presumably the Washington Wizards, perhaps someone else who gets bitten by the injury bug -- just to make it back into the Play-In Tournament picture. Even if they're there, their road to and through the playoffs becomes enormously precarious. It doesn't matter how dangerous you are in a playoff setting if you can't actually survive the regular season and make it there. It's too early to say that's where Indiana is headed, but the danger is very real.

    Snyder's Soapbox: Until MLB owners open the books, there's no reason to listen to pleas of poverty

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Here, I pontificate about matters related to Major League Baseball on a weekly basis.
    • In a recent development, the world of Major League Baseball -- which includes fans and media, too -- has something rather heavy hanging over its head this offseason.
    • People are going to take sides, and I make no apologies for being firmly on the players' side.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to Snyder's Soapbox! Here, I pontificate about matters related to Major League Baseball on a weekly basis. Some of the topics will be pressing matters, some might seem insignificant in the grand scheme of things, and most will be somewhere in between. The good thing about this website is that it's free, and you are allowed to click away. If you stay, you'll get smarter, though. That's a money-back guarantee. Let's get to it.

    In a recent development, the world of Major League Baseball -- which includes fans and media, too -- has something rather heavy hanging over its head this offseason. Obviously. We know all about that pesky CBA expiration on Dec. 1 and we know that the owners are all but certain to lock the players out that night while they push for a salary cap in the name of parity.

    People are going to take sides, and I make no apologies for being firmly on the players' side. They are the talent and why we watch the games. No one is buying owners' jerseys and sitting in the ballpark facing the suites.

    According to recent reports, another reason I'm not a huge fan, in general, of the owners is that I don't believe we're ever getting the full truth about how much money they make. The Braves are publicly traded and we can see a good breakdown of how they fared in 2025. The short version is that they are swimming in money. We could look at the two recently sold MLB teams for a hint, too. The Angels were sold for $4 billion; Arte Moreno bought the team for $184 million in 2003. The Padres were also sold recently for $3.9 billion. The San Diego media market size ranks ahead of only Kansas City, Cincinnati, Milwaukee and, eventually, Las Vegas among MLB cities.

    Recent findings suggest that and, again, sometimes you'll have an owner say the quiet part out loud. Enter Orioles owner David Rubenstein:.

    Sources indicate that "A lot of my friends were buying teams, and I realized they're making money. They're making more money than I'm making in private equity," Rubenstein stated last month at a forum with other pro sports owners at the Economic Club of Washington, D.C.

    " ... I couldn't figure out why it is that people who are fans are so obsessed with the success of their local team. They're not going to make any more money. They're not going to go to the Super Bowl and get a trophy out of it.".

    People who cape for the owners: this is what you are defending.

    It has been revealed that obviously every owner shouldn't be painted with the same brush. Some of them are legitimately fans. But I'd be willing to wager pretty heavily that a majority of the owners think like Rubenstein here and view the teams simply as vehicles to make as much money as possible.

    Do we even need to bother with the suggestion that we shouldn't care about our favorite teams since they don't make us money and we don't get pieces of metal trophies? Sports fandom can be one of the purest and most wholesome things about our society. It brings families and friends together. It gives us emotions we otherwise couldn't even possibly imagine feeling. And I'll say this, too: I've seen my favorite team win the World Series and the absolute last thing on my mind was, "man, I'd sure like a trophy for my own mantle." The memories can't be matched by anything material at all. I would take nothing of real, tangible substance over those memories.

    It's maddening that an owner can be so out of touch with the product that he purchased.

    Industry observers note that do please hone in on the money comment, though. That's a much bigger deal. We've heard owners of some smaller-market teams cry poor for years and even decades, and the response from the MLBPA every single time is a pretty simple one. I reached out to a source and heard it again: "If any team wants us to believe they are losing money, they can simply open their books.".

    Recent findings suggest that yes. The Braves have to and we can see how much of a money machine they are in the 11th-ranked media market (counting the two-team cities twice).

    Recent findings suggest that again, there will be exceptions, but the owners generally just view their teams as virtual ATMs, the output of which would be even higher with artificially decreased payroll because of a salary cap. At least one of them doesn't even understand why we care as much as we do.

    I remain firmly and proudly Team MLBPA.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It's fitting that this Week 12 slate coincides with the Thanksgiving holiday because it's going to feel like a five-course dinner.

    It has been revealed that starting on Wednesday, the NFL will be front and center for five of the following six days. We kick things off with the Green Bay Packers and Los Angeles Rams, featuring the return of Micah Parsons. Then, we have games on Thanksgiving, Black Friday, our typical Sunday slate, and, of course, "Monday Night Football." If you're not thankful for that heavy dose of football, then I don't know what to tell you.

    According to recent reports, naturally, there will be some twists and turns along the way as we embark on the marathon, which will almost certainly include an upset or two. Last week, we clued you in on the Philadelphia Eagles and New York Jets as underdogs that could pull off the outright upset, and they proved us right. Now, we'll look to Week 12, comb through this monstrous slate, and highlight five teams that could be on upset alert.

    It has been revealed that as is tradition, the Lions will be on our television this Thanksgiving. Surprisingly, when they kick off from Ford Field this holiday, they'll do so as a home underdog, currently laying 2.5 points to the rival Chicago Bears. The Lions are a perfect 5-0 at home this season, and Thursday's contest will be the first time in 2026 when they'll be a home dog. Historically, Detroit has done pretty well against the Bears, winning seven of their last eight games against them and outscoring them by 9.0 PPG over that stretch.

    They're riding a four-game winning streak at home over the Bears, where they've averaged 36.8 points per game and 439.5 total yards per game. More recently, they've swept Chicago in each of the last two seasons, including last year against former offensive coordinator Ben Johnson. Over that stretch, Jared Goff has thrown 11 touchdowns and just one interception, while averaging 305.5 passing yards per game.

    If they want to keep that pristine record, Detroit will once again have to look to Jahmyr Gibbs to help, and the star back does have an advantageous matchup against the Bears. Entering Week 12, Chicago is giving up 4.5 yards per carry this season, which is tied for the sixth-highest in the NFL. Gibbs has tallied at least 100 scrimmage yards in four straight games against the Bears.

    If the Lions come anywhere close to these prior averages, they shouldn't be considered a home dog.

    Industry observers note that it's somehow flying under the radar, but Patrick Mahomes looks like he's back to full strength. Of course, the Chiefs quarterback has become a runaway favorite for Comeback Player of the Year after tearing his ACL and LCL last year and starting right out of the gate for Kansas City. That was impressive on its own. Now, Mahomes is not just setting himself up for the CPOY award, but he could even be making a late push for MVP. Over his last four games, Mahomes has been nothing short of dominant, totaling 13 touchdowns and zero interceptions.

    Recent findings suggest that mahomes leveling up comes just in time for Kansas City's pivotal road matchup against the Bills to cap off the Thanksgiving slate. His stellar run will be put to the test, as the Bills' defense has not allowed a touchdown in 15 straight quarters heading into Week 12. That noted, the competition that Buffalo has faced over this stellar run hasn't been that fierce. Mahomes is a different animal entirely.

    Famously, Mahomes and Josh Allen are knotted at 5-5 against one another entering their 11th duel on Thursday night. Buffalo has seen all of their success against Mahomes come in the regular season, so this would be a rare victory for Kansas City. That stated, the defense is playing well enough to possibly contain Allen and Co. just enough to help Mahomes edge out the victory. This season, Kansas City is tied for the third-fewest yards allowed per play (4.9) and has the best red zone defense in the NFL (36% touchdown rate).

    In a recent development, the Seahawks are the more rested team heading into the NFC West matchup, an advantage that shouldn't be overlooked. Seattle was on the bye in Week 11, while the Niners were playing an international game in Mexico City against the Vikings. That alone should give the Seahawks a little bit of a leg up. However, the biggest reason to back them to possibly upset the 49ers is that they're the more desperate team.

    Seattle enters Week 12 on the fringe of the playoff picture as the No. 8 seed. Depending on what happens during the Thanksgiving Eve contest between the Packers (the No. 7 seed) and Rams (the No. 9 seed), there could be a window for them to rise up in the standings. If they lose, their hopes of repeating as Super Bowl champs could start to slip away.

    It has been revealed that when these two faced one another back in Week 5, the 49ers rolled into Lumen Field and picked up a win. Sam Darnold, who is scheduled to make his return this week after missing two games with injury, wasn't his best in that contest. He completed 18-of-29 for 195 yards, a touchdown and two interceptions. Despite that, Seattle hung around and nearly put themselves in an opportunity to go for the win or force overtime, but a controversial spot on a fourth-down completion to Cooper Kupp ended the game.

    This time around, the Seahawks should get much better production from their rushing attack now that Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price are back in the fold. Without either of them in Week 5, they averaged 3.4 yards per carry as a team. If they can get more of a consistent ground attack, that'll only help Darnold in the passing game.

    According to recent reports, it hasn't been perfect, but I like what I've seen out of Fernando Mendoza over his first two starts. The No. 1 overall pick was put in a rough spot in his first two games as QB1, with home games against the Seattle Seahawks and then the Broncos in Denver. Last week he completed just 48.6% of his passes, but there were flashes as he also tossed for 267 yards and three touchdowns as he tried to keep Las Vegas in the game. He also didn't have Brock Bowers as the starting tight end, who was sidelined with an ankle injury. Cleveland gives up the same amount of yards per play (5.2) as the Broncos, so this will be another tough test for Mendoza on Sunday.

    However, the Browns have almost exclusively been in one-score games. All six of their wins have been by four points or less, while eight of their 10 games have been decided by one score. With it constantly coming down to the wire, all Mendoza may need to do is make one or two special throws late, which he's more than capable of when accounting for his heroics at Indiana last year.

    In a recent development, on top of being intrigued by Mendoza, I'm also curious to see if Ashton Jeanty can build off of arguably his best game of the season. Against Denver, Jeanty rushed for 79 yards and caught five of his eight targets for 90 yards and a touchdown. This season, the Browns are giving up 126.3 rushing yards per game, which is the ninth-highest in the NFL. Their 4.6 yards per carry allowed is tied for the fifth-highest. If Jeanty can take advantage of this matchup, that only makes things easier for Mendoza, who is eyeing his first career win as a starter.

    It has been revealed that for whatever reason, the Dolphins own the Jets. Miami is 1-9 on the season and that lone victory came back in Week 7 when they rolled up to East Rutherford and took down New York, 28-25. While Kyle McCord will now be at quarterback compared to Malik Willis, who started that game earlier this year, the Dolphins' success against the Jets goes beyond 2026.

    They enter Week 12 on a 10-game winning streak at home against the Jets. Funny enough, the last road win the Jets had against the Dolphins came back in 2014 when ... Geno Smith was the quarterback. More recently, the Dolphins are 17-4 against the Jets since 2016, tied for the third-best record among division matchups over that span. Over the last two seasons, Miami is 3-0 against the Jets and 5-19 against every one else. That's the definition of having someone's number.

    Sources indicate that moreover, Aaron Glenn hasn't proven that he can beat any division rival, as the Jets head coach is 0-9 in his career against the AFC East with a -16.8 PPG differential. He'd become the fourth head coach in NFL history to start a career 0-10 vs. divisional opponents. Until he proves otherwise, it's wise to roll with the trend and take the value with Miami.

    MLB CBA negotiations timeline: League, MLBPA trade latest proposals over revenue sharing as Dec. 1 deadline nears

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • It has been revealed that the collective bargaining agreement, or CBA (or Basic Agreement, as it's known in a formal sense), is the negotiated accord between players and clubs -- i.e., the team owners and commissioner Rob Manfred, who represents their interests -- that governs the working relationship between the two parties, typically for a period of five years.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As the 2026 Major League Baseball offseason continues to unfold, something vitally notable to the future of the sport quietly hums in the background: the ongoing negotiations over a new collective bargaining agreement.

    It has been revealed that the collective bargaining agreement, or CBA (or Basic Agreement, as it's known in a formal sense), is the negotiated accord between players and clubs -- i.e., the team owners and commissioner Rob Manfred, who represents their interests -- that governs the working relationship between the two parties, typically for a period of five years. It covers things as mundane as players' meal allowances and travel protocols and as vital as minimum salaries, the structure of free agency, revenue-sharing specifics, and roster sizes. Every CBA can be distilled down to a fight over money, or, more specifically, how the league's revenues will be divided between players and team owners.

    According to recent reports, the first CBA covered the 1968 and 1969 seasons and was the first in professional sports history. That was the handiwork of Marvin Miller, the pioneering head of the Players Association (i.e., the players union) and belated Hall of Famer. It was Miller's organizing skills, foresight, and training as a union economist that allowed him to make the Players Association a viable and effective labor organization. Every CBA negotiation from 1972 through 1994-95 resulted in some form and scale of labor stoppage, whether a players' strike or an owner-implemented lockout. After the cancellation of the 1994 World Series because of the worst labor stoppage in the sport's history, a long run of peace followed. That peace lasted until the prior CBA negotiations, which resulted in a 99-day lockout forced by team owners and delayed the start of the 2022 season.

    The current CBA negotiations have been underway for some time, and not surprisingly, the two sides remain far apart on several key issues. The biggest fight will be over the owners' renewed desire to implement a salary cap, which the union continues to view as a non-starter. The push for a cap has less to do with the notions of competitive balance and more to do with the ownership's internal belief that being the only non-salary-capped league among the major North American sports is harming franchise values. The cap, though, is but one of many pressing issues on which players and owners must find congruity.

    Moving forward, the process will be uncertain and rife with posturing and pointed public comments from both sides. The hope, though, is that a newly introduced CBA will be agreed to before the middle of March 2027, at which point there's a high risk of having the 2027 season delayed or even abbreviated.

    It has been revealed that to keep you informed of the twists and turns along the way to a new CBA, we've provided a detailed timeline of negotiations. That timeline will illuminate the vital and finer points of the talks and, along the way, explain the implications of the various proposals coming from each side. The hope, of course, is that all of it culminates in a timely agreement that permits a fully intact and on-time 2027 season.

    In earlier iterations of negotiations, MLB proposed a salary-escrow system like the ones found in the NBA and NHL. This would mean a percentage of player salaries is withheld in case league revenue projections fall short for a given year. If that's the case, then that money in escrow goes back to the league to cover the revenue shortfalls. If revenues are higher than projected, that excess is shared with the players. The MLBPA has pointedly opposed the escrow system on the grounds that it undermines the notion of guaranteed player salaries. In its latest statement on the negotiations, MLB withdrew the escrow proposal. "For months, union leadership has attacked the escrow provision used in other sports and mischaracterized the concern as the end of guaranteed contracts," MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin mentioned in a statement. "MLB took another step today by withdrawing our escrow proposal, removing any doubt that every single guaranteed player contract will remain fully guaranteed in the newly introduced salary cap and floor system.".

    The specifics of the new proposal, which like all other league proposals thus far been tied to the players' accceptance of a cap and floor on team payrolls:.

    In response, interim union head Bruce Meyer released the following statement:.

    It has been revealed that "MLB today modified its salary cap proposal to 'eliminate' escrow, but once again it provides no real benefit under their proposed cap system. Instead of holding back player money each year, MLB's upcoming proposal is to take that same amount of money out of players' pockets in the following year. It's a different way of achieving the same objective of the salary cap - to reduce and suppress player salaries and freedom of movement. This is yet another example of how MLB's salary cap proposal pits player against player, past, present, and future.".

    It has been revealed that in their latest bargaining session, the MLBPA maintained its previous proposals aimed to increase revenue sharing support for small market teams, including a mechanism designed to punish teams that do not put revenue sharing funds into the roster. The union also mentioned the proposal is designed to remove "any league excuses for the continuation of blackouts.".

    Here are the details of the union's latest proposal:.

    As for MLB's proposal, it now includes a $1 million minimum salary (previous proposals were described as $1 million but not quite that amount), and a upcoming series of bonuses for all player classes:.

    MLB's proposal is once again tied to the MLBPA's acceptance of a salary cap/floor system, which the players association has insisted it will never allow.

    "The league's proposals today don't add a single dollar in overall player compensation as compared to prior proposals, and once again are expressly conditioned on accepting their salary cap and other anti-player restrictions," MLBPA executive director Bruce Meyer noted in a statement. "Any supposed benefits to certain classes of players are simply taken out of the pockets of other players and are vastly outweighed by the negative effects of the cap and MLB's other restrictions. These negative effects include, but are not limited to, a drastic reduction in overall player compensation and benefits, the end of fully guaranteed contracts, and dramatic restrictions on players' career choices and freedom to contract.".

    Industry observers note that the MLBPA on Friday put forth a series of proposed changes to the international signing structure. Notably, the union did not propose the implementation of an international draft, which the league has long sought. "We are committed to negotiating a system that preserves opportunities for future generations of players, protects young prospects from exploitation, and provides flexibility without further burdening international players with new artificial restrictions like a draft," MLBPA interim leader Bruce Meyer mentioned in a statement released by the union. "Our proposals help build upon baseball's advances as an international game, while safeguarding the interests of young athletes who are the future of our sport.".

    Specifically, the union's proposal calls for:.

    It has been revealed that also on Friday, MLB removed from the bargaining table an earlier proposal to exclude high school players from the annual MLB Draft. MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin said the following in a statement released by the league, which also includes a call for the implementation of an international draft:.

    "In recognition of the feedback we received from the MLBPA on our domestic amateur proposal, we made a concession today by withdrawing our proposal on high school eligibility and proposed to maintain the current entry rules for domestic amateurs. On the international system, we continue to believe it is long past time to reform the system in ways that would address longstanding challenges and benefit future players. The enhanced transparency of the International Draft that we have proposed best addresses the root causes of corruption in the current system.".

    Speaking to the media at the owners meetings in Newly introduced York, MLB commissioner Rob Manfred said while there's room for compromise in general with the MLBPA, there's no room for compromise on the proposed cap and floor on team payrolls. "The owners want a deal with a salary cap and floor," he said.

    In a recent development, "I can't imagine the owners ratifying a deal that does not include a cap and floor," Manfred also said. "... Thirty clubs are 100 percent unanimous in support of the proposals that have been made. I'm not in a position to speculate about what happens in the event that we don't achieve our overriding objective, which is to get a cap and floor system that addresses the competitive problem that our fans perceive.".

    MLBPA interim head Bruce Meyer, who has insisted that the union will never accept a salary cap, pushed back again.

    "There can be no clearer example of the league's lack of seriousness than their insistence that they will not negotiate over the economics outside of a radical change to the system that would dramatically reduce overall player compensation for all categories of players and strip fundamental rights from players like the ability to have truly guaranteed contracts," he noted Wednesday in a statement.

    "There should be no illusions about the owners' true motivation in pushing for this system. They want to make more money in profits and franchise values by artificially suppressing player salaries.".

    It has been revealed that to date, the league has tied every individual proposal to the players' acceptance of a cap-and-floor system. The players through their union have historically shown no willingness to discuss a cap on payrolls.

    MLB Players Association executive director Bruce Meyer stated MLB is not serious about preventing the lockout and has "wasted months of time" trying to court public opinion when the two sides could have been having substantive negotiations.

    "At the end of the day, this is going to come down to the bargaining table," Meyer told the Boston Globe. "And we have been for months, since May, looking for a serious partner in negotiations, and the league has insisted since May that they won't negotiate over anything economic outside of our agreement to a salary cap. In that respect, we've wasted months of time when we could have been having a serious negotiation. So I'd say the more the league is focused on things other than bargaining with us in good faith, I would say that's counterproductive.".

    Meyer also mentioned the MLBPA has put forth proposals intended to promote competitive balance and correct the game's revenue disparity, but the owners are focused on a salary cap to "increase their profits and franchise values." He added that the two sides have made progress on non-economic matters, such as drug testing and gambling policies.

    To allow for a "smoother transition" to a salary cap/floor system, MLB proposed delaying its implementation until 2028. That would give teams time to prepare and get their payrolls in order, and allow for a full offseason heading into the system. The current competitive balance tax and revenue sharing system would remain in place in 2027.

    In a recent development, "We recognize that clubs will need a full offseason to prepare to operate within the cap and floor system. Therefore, with this offseason already underway, we proposed today to begin the cap and floor system in 2028," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "This proposal would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system.".

    In a recent development, MLB also upped its salary cap/floor proposal to $258.3 million and $180.2 million, respectively. Back in June, the league proposed a $245.3 million cap and $171.2 million floor. It states it is willing to discuss further phase-in scenarios for a salary cap/floor system.

    In its latest proposal, MLB proposed reducing the regular season from 162 games to 154 games, and adding a standard off day to every week. The league also proposed extending the Division Series from a best-of-five to a best-of-seven, and allowing higher seeded teams to select their opponents in the Wild Card Series and Division Series. As with every MLB proposal to date, the 154-game schedule and changes to the postseason format are contingent on the MLBPA accepting a salary car/floor system.

    If labor strife lops off 60 or more games from the 2027 MLB season, then the consequences could be significant. The Athletic recently reported that if the forthcoming lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That's significant because commissioner Rob Manfred hopes to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that latest media rights structure. As such, this is a heavy incentive, at least on the league side, to not let any labor stoppage drag into June.

    Sources indicate that A poll of current MLB players across the full spectrum of salaries and service time conducted by ESPN showed strong resistance to the payroll cap and floor being demanded by ownership and league and being put forth as a precondition to every proposed change from that side. An excerpt:.

    How open are you to a salary cap?NL starting pitcher entering arbitration: Not open.

    Recent findings suggest that NL infielder making eight figures annually: Zero. No chance.

    Industry observers note that NL infielder on two-year contract: Zero. Absolute zero.

    Sources indicate that NL pre-arbitration journeyman: From what I've been told, I don't think it's good for the game. I just don't know if I know all the pros and cons of it. But, from everything we've been told, it doesn't sound like it's a good thing.

    NL reliever on multiyear contract: With the right criteria, I'd be open to it.

    AL starting pitcher in arbitration: I don't want it. In '94, they canceled the World Series, so if those guys can miss over half a year and miss the World Series, I think we're fully prepared to hold out for sure.

    AL catcher entering arbitration: I need more information, but perhaps I would listen on it.

    That's mostly strong sentiment that aligns with the MLBPA position on the cap, but it's not ironclad. MLB in negotiations and its public statements is seeking to tap into any existing divide between, broadly speaking, lower-salaried players with not much service time and more tenured veterans in their higher-earning years. There is a bit of a schism there, but it would take a substantial one to shift, in any exploitable way, the union's long-standing opposition to a cap-and-floor system. The ESPN piece covers an array of CBA topics. With the two questions related to the proposed cap, the responses can be broken down as 16 in mostly firm opposition to a cap and five not necessarily in favor but open to further discussions and reflection.

    MLB proposed a series of changes to current roster rules that, in a statement, the league says are aimed at "creating more stability in rosters, getting the best players to the Major Leagues more promptly, and accelerating the pace of the offseason." Among the rule changes included in MLB's proposal are:.

    All the proposed roster rule changes are contingent on the MLB Players Association agreeing to a salary cap-and-floor system.

    During a negotiating session with the league, the players' union puts forth its own proposed changes to the MLB Draft -- changes that are, in essence, a rejoinder to the drastic overhaul earlier put forward by MLB. Among the changes the MLBPA proposes are:.

    Additionally, the union proposes increasing the money payable to draftees under the incentive bonus plan and eliminating, according to the MLBPA, "the current practice of clubs deducting certain bonuses from players' continuing education benefits.".

    In a recent development, the timing of the draft has actually been a concern for front offices for years, since it was shifted later in the calendar to coincide with the All-Star break in 2021. Holding the draft in July crams both that and the trade deadline into just a few weeks and making it more difficult to allocate resources.

    In a recent development, commissioner Rob Manfred and interim union head Bruce Meyer each hold press conferences on the day of the All-Star Game in Philadelphia. "I think that I have an ownership group that is more united than any group in my entire time of baseball," Manfred indicates, referring at least obliquely to the league's push for a salary cap. "They are a group that believes in what I am arguing for.".

    "The supposed stewards of the game have spent an inordinate amount of time trying to convince those same fans that they don't have hope or they shouldn't have hope or that the product that they're paying to consume in record numbers is somehow broken," Meyer claims of MLB's efforts to highlight perceived competitive-balance challenges in the face of increasing attendance and television ratings. "I think it's perverse.".

    The MLBPA puts forth multiple proposals, many of them dealing with procedural matters for purposes of player health, safety, and wellness. They include:.

    The union's latest proposal is a reminder of the breadth of CBA discussions. Most problems are not the big-ticket items like a salary cap or lack thereof or revenue sharing structure but instead are somewhat esoteric matters that strike most fans as mundane. To players and teams, though, they're important considerations and in some instances may even provide a foundation of common ground moving forward.

    Industry observers note that more face-to-face negotiations take place, and MLB proposes more changes to the free-agency system, among other asks. MLB's latest proposal includes the following, all of which depend upon the union's acceptance of a payroll cap:.

    Recent findings suggest that MLB in a prior proposal called for a cap on team payrolls of $245.3 million starting in 2027 and a payroll floor of $171.2 million. The league challenges a statement that reads in full:.

    Industry observers note that "The biggest concern baseball fans want solved to strengthen the game is fixing the payroll disparity that leaves too many fans without hope of their team competing for a World Series title. Every other major U.S. sport has tackled this problem, and every year more small market teams in those leagues have a chance to win. The salary cap and floor proposal levels the playing field, allowing us greater flexibility to address longstanding player priorities while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50/50.

    In a recent development, "Today, in addition to proposing the largest ever increase in the minimum salary, earned by over half of MLB players, we accepted two landmark changes to free agency that have been in place for 50 years. We agreed to both the MLBPA's proposal to provide earlier access to free agency, and their proposal to eliminate the qualifying offer system, a provision players view as a drag on free agency. We also proposed to eliminate deferred compensation and to create a latest 'Cornerstone Player' provision similar to the NBA's 'Bird Rights' to give every team a fair shot at retaining their fans' favorite star players.

    "We will continue working with the MLBPA during the bargaining process to improve the game for teams, players and fans.".

    "After making a series of proposals to reduce player compensation by billions of dollars, eliminate fundamental rights with a salary cap, and destroy the amateur entry process, Major League Baseball and team owners are now attempting to distract from the true impact their proposal would have on baseball. These misleading offers are designed to look like 'improvements' but are of little or no value, given they are expressly conditioned on agreement to the league's cap system which eliminates the free market, and ensures gains for one player only come at the expense of another.

    In a recent development, "The league also introduced a litany of additional restrictions on player rights — limiting salaries, contract length, performance, award, and signing bonuses. While MLB claims to be acting in the interest of fans, their proposals thus far are entirely consistent with owners' long-held goals: suppressing player salaries and maximizing club profits.

    Sources indicate that "Owners' attempts to pit players against players are nothing fresh, but they've failed in the past and will fail again now, because PA members remain unified. We are committed to achieving a fair deal that protects the rights of all players, promotes competition, and leaves our game better for future generations.".

    Lacking from the league's latest proposal, at least on the public-facing side, is any revisiting of the recent changes to the draft and any mention of prior proposed changes to the league's revenue-sharing system.

    During these same face-to-face sessions, the MLBPA proposes a ban on prop bets placed on individual players, ESPN reports. The idea is to preempt harrassment of players by gamblers. The proposed ban would extend to bets placed on individual player performance prior to and during any MLB game. The MLBPA also requested that players be permitted to engage in paid endorsements and sponsorships with sportsbooks and prediction markets.

    MLB and the MLBPA meet for face-to-face negotiations, and owners propose sweeping changes to the draft and also push for an international draft. As for the MLB Draft, formally known as the First-Year Player Draft, MLB pushes for the following changes:.

    Industry observers note that "Over the last several years, college baseball has undergone a remarkable transformation," MLB claims in a statement. "Expanded scholarships, NIL opportunities, revenue sharing and significant investments in facilities and player development have made college baseball an increasingly important pathway that is producing major league-ready talent at an accelerated rate. Today's top programs provide players with resources, competition and national exposure that were unimaginable a decade ago. Our proposal is designed to build on that momentum to benefit the game at the college, minor-league and major-league levels. By creating a draft system centered around college-aged players and making most college players eligible one year earlier, more players will benefit from both a college education and an elite development environment while reaching professional baseball -- and ultimately the major leagues -- more quickly. We believe these changes will strengthen college baseball and deepen fans' connection to the next generation of major league stars. We look forward to working with the MLBPA throughout the bargaining process to modernize the domestic amateur system in a way that benefits players, clubs, and fans.".

    As for the international draft, MLB proposed making players outside of the U.S., Puerto Rico, and Canada (who are already included in the standard draft) subject to a similar system. The international draft would, as with the proposed changes to the MLB Draft, come with a $200 million bonus cap. At present, international amateurs may sign with any team under the international free agent system, although teams do have hard budget caps each year.

    The MLBPA also issues a statement in response to MLB's proposals:.

    Today, MLB made another set of proposals that are flat out bad for baseball, ones that would cripple the next generation of players and damage the future of our game. They would, among other things:.

    Players remain committed to bargaining in good faith and leaving baseball better than they found it -- the league's proposals fall woefully short.

    U.S. President Donald J. Trump publicly supports MLB's efforts to implement a salary cap. "If you don't have a salary cap, you don't have a sport, because they can't help themselves," Trump says. "Football has a salary cap. They should have done it a long time ago.

    According to recent reports, "It's shocking, frankly, that they didn't put a cap on many years ago," he noted, possibly referencing the 1994-95 strike. "They had a chance to do a cap, but they blew it.".

    In a recent development, speaking to reporters following the owners' quarterly meetings, Manfred addresses the luxury-tax system he and the owners seek to replace with a cap. "We have tried mightily over several rounds of bargaining to use a competitive balance (luxury) tax to address competitive concerns," Manfred says. "And sometimes you've got to admit you failed.

    "We made a proposal on one set of topics. At the outset of negotiations, I went and said myself, 'We're open to whatever ideas people have, but we need a realistic framework that addresses the fans' concerns about competitive balance.' You just can't ignore that financial penalties have not gotten it done for us.".

    In a call with reporters, MLBPA interim executive director Bruce Meyer addresses the owners' proposals. "Using MLB's definition of revenue and player share as set forth in their proposal and their presentation to us, player share under their proposal would go down," Meyer states. "Player share for this season, 2026, is projected to be well over 50 percent, using, again MLB's definitions of revenues and what counts against player share.

    "Had MLB's proposal been in place in 2026, players, we estimate, would lose over half a billion dollars.".

    Meyer also refers to a salary cap as "a form of institutionalized collusion.".

    "Our salary cap-and-floor proposal addresses our fans' concerns by leveling the playing field while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50-50 like the other leagues," MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin responded on behalf of the league. "Under our proposal, major-league players will receive more compensation in year one of the system than in 2026. We are ready to listen if the MLBPA wants to counter our proposal at the bargaining table.".

    According to recent reports, MLB and the owners publicly announce their first formal CBA proposal. Chiefly, they propose:.

    Sources indicate that using competitive balance tax (CBT), or luxury tax, payrolls as a guide, since they include benefits expenses, nine teams at present would be above the proposed cap line, while 12 teams would be below the floor. However, as Craig Goldstein points out, the amount needed to get all these teams below or above the relevant payroll thresholds amounts to an $18.7 million loss in aggregate player salary overall. Another sticking point will be how league revenues are defined. Owners no doubt seek to carve out things like real estate developments surrounding ballparks and ownership stakes in regional sports. As well, MLB's working definition of league revenues includes many expense deductions.

    On another level, the fact that Manfred is able to persuade large-market, high-revenue clubs to agree to equal sharing of all local revenues is a notable development. However, such a concession by those large-market clubs may be contingent upon the implementation of a cap.

    Another sticking point is that the league proposes an escrow system, as is used in the NBA and the NHL. This would mean a percentage of player salaries is withheld. If revenues fall short of projections, some of that money in escrow goes back to the league. If revenues are higher than projected, that excess is shared with the players. The MLBPA opposes the escrow system on the grounds that it undermines the notion of guaranteed player salaries.

    The MLBPA makes an opening suite of proposals to the league, including:.

    "Today, the MLBPA (Major League Baseball Players Association) presented a comprehensive set of economic proposals designed to advance the rights and benefits of players at all levels," Meyer claims in a statement released by the union. "Our goal is to preserve and improve baseball's market system, rewarding competition on and off the field. Additionally, the players' proposals provide increased revenue sharing initially guaranteeing every small market club a minimum of $240m in revenue every season. This enhanced revenue sharing includes added protections to ensure clubs prioritize winning over profiteering. Ultimately, our proposals are designed to build upon the incredible momentum and popularity of our sport world-wide.".

    In a recent development, "We appreciate the union making a set of proposals and we look forward to continuing the bargaining process and working towards solving the competitive balance problem our fans are telling us needs to be addressed," Caplin states in a statement. "We understand their proposals are designed to benefit players. Unfortunately, they do not address and in fact exacerbate the competitive balance problem our fans are telling us we must address. The MLBPA's proposal would reduce the amount transferred to lower-revenue Clubs, weaken the Competitive Balance Tax, and lead to even more payroll disparity than exists today. For example, under the Union's proposal, the Dodgers would pay less in luxury tax payments, giving them an additional $70 million to spend on payroll.".

    Negotiations on a latest CBA formally begin between teams and players. Among the key issues to be discussed will be the league's desire for a salary cap, drastic changes to the revenue sharing system, league expansion, possible further playoff expansion, and an international draft.

    The 2022-26 Basic Agreement is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET, at which point owners are expected to lock out the players in the absence of a upcoming agreement.
